h1: Solar Panel Cleaning Loss Calculator: Dust and When to Clean
author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: kwp
fields.label: Solar system size
fields.hint: Total panel kW on the roof (panels × panel watts ÷ 1000), from your installer's quote.

fields.name: yield
fields.label: Units one kW of panels makes a day
fields.hint: The default is the yearly average for Lahore. Your inverter app shows your own: units a day ÷ system kW on a clear day after cleaning.

fields.name: days
fields.label: Days since the last cleaning or good rain
fields.hint: A heavy rain washes most dust off; count from then if it was more recent than the last cleaning.

fields.name: tariff
fields.label: Value of one unit
fields.hint: Units you use yourself are worth your slab rate (the default is the Pakistan unprotected rate for 301 to 400 units). Exported units are worth the buyback rate instead.

fields.name: cleaning_cost
fields.label: Cost of one cleaning
fields.hint: Example figure. Enter what a cleaner charges for your roof, or the cost of water and your own time.

fields.name: rate
fields.label: Dust loss per day
fields.hint: Share of output lost to dust each day without rain, as a decimal, not a percent: 0.003 means 0.3% a day; typing 0.3 would mean 30% a day and is rejected. The default is an estimate for dusty Pakistani cities, not a measurement; measure your own by comparing output before and after a cleaning on two clear days.

answer: Dust left for {{in.days|int}} days on a {{in.kwp|int}} kW solar system in Lahore cuts output by about {{out.soiling|pct}}: {{out.loss_kwh_day|1}} units a day, worth {{out.rs_lost_day|rs}} at {{in.tariff|rs2}} per unit. Loss = kW × daily yield × dust share, with the dust share growing about {{d.soiling_rate_per_day|pct}} a day. A {{in.cleaning_cost|rs}} cleaning pays for itself about every {{out.clean_after_days|int}} days.
how: Dust share: {{out.rate|pct}} a day × {{out.days}} days = {{out.soiling|pct}} (never more than {{d.soiling_cap|pct}}, where dust stops building up much). Units lost: {{out.kwp|1}} kW × {{out.yield|1}} units per kW a day × {{out.soiling|pct}} = {{out.loss_kwh_day|1}} units a day. Money lost: {{out.loss_kwh_day|1}} × {{out.tariff|rs2}} = {{out.rs_lost_day|rs}} a day. Cleaning pays when the money lost since the last cleaning, added up day by day, passes the cost of one cleaning.
key_facts: Solar output lost to dust = system kW × units per kW a day × dust share; by Wattlyst's estimate for dusty Pakistani cities the dust share grows about {{d.soiling_rate_per_day|pct}} a day without rain, up to about {{d.soiling_cap|pct}}.

A {{in.kwp|int}} kW system in Lahore left {{in.days|int}} days without cleaning loses about {{out.loss_kwh_day|1}} units a day, {{out.rs_lost_day|rs}} a day at the unprotected rate of {{in.tariff|rs2}} per unit.

With a cleaning cost of {{in.cleaning_cost|rs}}, cleaning a {{in.kwp|int}} kW system in Lahore pays for itself about every {{out.clean_after_days|int}} days; a {{ex.2.in.kwp|int}} kW system that exports most of its units, valued at the buyback rate, takes about {{ex.2.out.clean_after_days|int}} days.

The dust rate is an estimate: dust in a city next to a busy road, a brick kiln or a construction site builds faster, and a monsoon shower resets it; compare your inverter app's output on clear days before and after a cleaning to measure your own.

formula.text: Loss a day = kWp × yield × min(rate × days, cap); clean when Σ daily loss × tariff > cleaning cost
lines: kWp = panel kW installed; yield = units one kW makes a day in your city
rate = share of output lost to dust per day without rain (estimate, editable)
days = days since the last cleaning or heavy rain; cap = the most dust takes off
tariff = Rs per unit: your slab rate for units you use, the buyback rate for units you export
Cleaning interval = first day the money lost since cleaning, added day by day, passes the cleaning cost

sections.h2: Solar panel dust loss: how much does dust really cost?
p: For the default {{in.kwp|int}} kW system in Lahore after {{in.days|int}} dry days, about {{out.soiling|pct}} of the output, {{out.loss_kwh_day|1}} units a day. The loss starts small and grows each day, because dust builds up until wind or rain removes it. After a few dry months it levels off near {{d.soiling_cap|pct}} in our estimate, as the last row of the table below shows.
Pakistan's dry months, from October to June outside the monsoon, are when dust matters most. Smog in the Punjab winter adds a sticky film that rain alone does not always remove.

sections.h2: How often to clean solar panels
p: Clean when the money lost since the last cleaning passes the cost of a cleaning. For the default system at {{in.cleaning_cost|rs}} a cleaning, that is about every {{out.clean_after_days|int}} days. A larger system loses more units each day, so it pays to clean it more often; a cheaper cleaning (your own hose and soft brush) also shortens the interval.
In the monsoon a heavy shower does much of the work, so count days from the last good rain. In a dusty dry spell, a cleaning every couple of weeks pays on large systems.

sections.h2: Exported units: use the buyback rate
p: If most of your daytime units are exported under net billing, each unit lost to dust is a unit you would have sold at the buyback rate, not one you would have bought at your slab rate. The third worked example values the loss at {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_rs_per_unit_default|rs2}} per unit, an estimate because NEPRA had not notified the rate when we checked: the loss in rupees is smaller and the cleaning interval longer.

sections.h2: How to clean solar panels safely
p: Clean early in the morning or in the evening, when the glass is cool: cold water on hot glass can crack it. Use clean water and a soft brush or sponge, no detergent, no pressure washer and no metal scraper; hard tap water can leave spots, so a final rinse with filtered water helps. Never walk on panels.
Most rooftops are reachable only from a ladder or a parapet. If yours is not safe to reach, a cleaning service is cheaper than a fall.

mistakes: Judging by eye. A thin even film of dust is hard to see and still costs output; compare the inverter app's units on two clear days before and after cleaning.
Cleaning at noon. Cold water on hot glass can crack a panel; clean in the early morning or evening.
Using detergent, a pressure washer or a hard brush. They can damage the anti-reflective coating and the frame seals, which costs more output than the dust did.
Valuing every lost unit at the slab rate on a system that exports most of its output. Exported units are worth the buyback rate.
safety: Panels sit on a roof, often at the edge: use a safe ladder, a harness where there is no parapet, and never stand on the panels. Do not spray water on the inverter, junction boxes or cable joints. If a panel is cracked or a cable is damaged, keep off it and call your installer or a licensed electrician.

faq.q: How much power do dirty solar panels lose?
faq.a: By our estimate about {{d.soiling_rate_per_day|pct}} of output for each dry day, levelling off near {{d.soiling_cap|pct}}. After {{in.days|int}} days that is {{out.soiling|pct}}, {{out.loss_kwh_day|1}} units a day on a {{in.kwp|int}} kW system in Lahore.

faq.q: How often should I clean my solar panels in Pakistan?
faq.a: When the money lost since the last cleaning passes the cleaning cost: about every {{out.clean_after_days|int}} days for a {{in.kwp|int}} kW system in Lahore at {{in.cleaning_cost|rs}} a cleaning. Large systems and dusty dry spells call for more often; the monsoon for less.

faq.q: Is it worth paying someone to clean solar panels?
faq.a: Yes when the system is large enough. A {{ex.2.in.kwp|int}} kW system recovers a {{ex.2.out.cleaning_cost|rs}} cleaning in about {{ex.2.out.clean_after_days|int}} days even at the buyback rate; a small system takes longer, so cleaning it yourself is cheaper.
A heavy rain removes most loose dust, so count days from the last good rain. A light drizzle can turn dust into mud spots, and winter smog leaves a film that needs a wipe.

faq.q: What is the best time to clean solar panels?
faq.a: Early morning or evening, when the glass is cool and the panels make little power. Use plain water and a soft brush, never detergent or a pressure washer.

faq.q: How do I measure my own dust loss?
faq.a: Note the units your inverter app shows on a clear day, clean the panels, and note the next clear day. The difference ÷ the first figure is your dust share; divide it by the days since the last cleaning for your own daily rate.
